questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
{y}^{″}-2{y}^{′}-8y=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -8 & =0 \\ (\lambda -4)(\lambda +2) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So $\lambda =-2$ or $\lambda =4$, and therefore the complementary function ${y}_{c}$ is

$$
y=A{e}^{-2x}+B{e}^{4x}.
$$

We now need to find the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $1.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular integral is also a polynomial of degree $1,$ i.e.

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha x+\beta 
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
{y}_{p}^{′}=\alpha ,\,{y}_{p}^{″}=0.
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation:

$$
0-2\alpha -8(\alpha x+\beta )=16x-4
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
-8\alpha x-(2\alpha +8\beta )=16x-4.
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}-8\alpha =16\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,x) \\ 2\alpha +8\beta =4\, & (\text{equating the constants})\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-2,\beta =1.$

Therefore, the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-2x+1.
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{-2x}+B{e}^{4x}-2x+1.
$$

Now let's find the constants $A$ and $B.$ 

Substituting $y(0)=2$ into the general solution gives

$$
A+B=1.
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(0)=8.$ First, we differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}:$

$$
{y}^{′}=-2A{e}^{-2x}+4B{e}^{4x}-2
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(0)=8$ into the above gives

$$
-2A+4B=10.
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations for $A$ and $B:$

$$
{\begin{aligned}A+B=1 \\ -2A+4B=10\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $A=-1,B=2.$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=-{e}^{-2x}+2{e}^{4x}-2x+1.
$$

questions.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+13y=39x+1.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+13y=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +13 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +4)-4+13 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)^{2}+9 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)^{2} & =-9 \\ \lambda -2 & =\pm 3\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =2\pm 3\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

So $\lambda =2\pm 3\text{i}$, and therefore the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)={e}^{2x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡3x).
$$

We now need to find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $1.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular integral is also a polynomial of degree $1,$ i.e.

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha x+\beta 
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=\alpha ,\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=0
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation:

$$
0-4\alpha +13(\alpha x+\beta )=39x+1
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
13\alpha x+(13\beta -4\alpha )=39x+1.
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}13\alpha =39\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,x) \\ 13\beta -4\alpha =1\, & (\text{equating the constants})\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =3,\beta =1.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=3x+1.
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y={e}^{2x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡3x)+3x+1.
$$

questions.problem:
Given that the differential equation 

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+3y=3{x}^{2}+2x+3
$$

has the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-x}+B{e}^{-3x}$, find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ to this equation.
questions.worked_solution:
The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $2.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $2,$ i.e.

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha {x}^{2}+\beta x+\gamma 
$$

where $\alpha ,$ $\beta ,$ and $\gamma $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=2\alpha x+\beta ,\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=2\alpha 
$$

To find the values of $\alpha ,$ $\beta $ and $\gamma ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation:

$$
2\alpha +4(2\alpha x+\beta )+3(\alpha {x}^{2}+\beta x+\gamma )=3{x}^{2}+2x+3
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives:

$$
3\alpha {x}^{2}+(8\alpha +3\beta )x+(2\alpha +4\beta +3\gamma )=3{x}^{2}+2x+3
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}3\alpha =3\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,{x}^{2}) \\ 8\alpha +3\beta =2\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,x) \\ 2\alpha +4\beta +3\gamma =3\, & (\text{equating the constants})\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =1,\beta =-2,\gamma =3.$

Therefore, the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x)$ is:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={x}^{2}-2x+3
$$

questions.problem:
Given that the differential equation 

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y=3x+4
$$

has the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-x}+Bx{e}^{-x}$, find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ to this equation.
questions.worked_solution:
The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $1.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $1,$ i.e.

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha x+\beta 
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=\alpha ,\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=0
$$

To find the values of $\alpha ,$  and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation:

$$
0+2\alpha +(\alpha x+\beta )=3x+4
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives:

$$
\alpha x+(2\alpha +\beta )=3x+4
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}\alpha =3\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,x) \\ 2\alpha +\beta =4\, & (\text{equating the constants})\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =3,\,\beta =-2.$

Therefore, the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=3x-2.
$$

questions.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+6\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+10y=5{x}^{2}-4x+5.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+6\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+10y=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda +10 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda +9)-9+10 & =0 \\ (\lambda +3)^{2}+1 & =0 \\ (\lambda +3)^{2} & =-1 \\ \lambda +3 & =\pm \text{i} \\ \lambda  & =-3\pm \text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

So $\lambda =-3\pm \text{i}$, and therefore the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)={e}^{-3x}(A\operatorname{cos}⁡x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡x).
$$

We now need to find the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $2.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular integral is also a polynomial of degree $2,$ i.e.

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha {x}^{2}+\beta x+\gamma 
$$

where $\alpha ,$ $\beta $, and $\gamma $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=2\alpha x+\beta ,\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=2\alpha .
$$

To find the values of $\alpha ,$ $\beta ,$ and $\gamma ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation. This gives:

$$
2\alpha +6(2\alpha x+\beta )+10(\alpha {x}^{2}+\beta x+\gamma )=5{x}^{2}-4x+5
$$

We then group the terms on the left-hand side, as follows:

$$
10\alpha {x}^{2}+(12\alpha +10\beta )x+(2\alpha +6\beta +10\gamma )=5{x}^{2}-4x+5
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}10\alpha =5\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,{x}^{2}) \\ 12\alpha +10\beta =-4\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,x) \\ 2\alpha +6\beta +10\gamma =5\, & (\text{equating the constants})\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =\frac{1}{2},\beta =-1,\gamma =1.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}-x+1.
$$

The general solution is given by 

$$
y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p}
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y={e}^{-3x}(A\operatorname{cos}⁡x+B\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}-x+1.
$$
